parts.partTitle: How HashMap Works Under the Hood

beats.headline: Why is HashMap initial capacity 16 and not 10?
beats.subline: HashMap doesn't use standard modulo division. It relies on bitwise mask magic.
beats.narration: If you pass 10 to a HashMap constructor, Java silently bumps it to 16. That power-of-two capacity lets HashMap replace slow remainder math with ultra-fast bitwise AND operations.

beats.title: Hash Perturbation & Bitwise Indexing
beats.subtitle: Converting key.hashCode() into a bucket array index

nodes.label: h ^ (h >>> 16)
nodes.detail: Spreads high bits down into low bits to prevent collisions

nodes.label: (n - 1) & hash
nodes.detail: Fast bitwise AND replaces modulo division in 1 CPU cycle

nodes.label: Node<K,V>[] table
nodes.detail: Directly places entry inside power-of-two bucket array

beats.narration: To pick a bucket index, HashMap perturbs the hash by shifting the top 16 bits into the bottom 16. Then it masks the hash with n minus 1, placing entries into buckets without integer division.

beats.title: Pre-Sizing Maps to Avoid Resizing

steps.explanation: HashMap.newHashMap computes exact capacity for target count taking default 0.75 load factor into account.
Standard constructor rounds up to next power of two but resizes early when size exceeds capacity times 0.75.

beats.narration: Every resize doubles the bucket array and redistributes existing entries. Java 19 introduced HashMap dot newHashMap, which computes the exact capacity required for your target count without triggering an expensive middle-of-the-road table resize.

beats.title: Modulo Division vs. Bitwise AND Masking

top.label: Standard Modulo Math
points: Works with arbitrary non-power-of-two array lengths

bottom.label: HashMap Bitwise AND Masking
bottom.code:
int hash = (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
int index = (table.length - 1) & hash;
points: Requires table capacity to remain strict power of two

beats.narration: Integer division takes multiple CPU cycles. When table length is a power of two, n minus one forms a bit mask where bitwise AND yields the exact remainder instantly.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Power-of-two capacity turns modulo into 1-cycle bitwise AND
High-bit shift perturbation prevents low-bit collision clustering
Java 19 HashMap.newHashMap calculates exact target capacity

beats.headline: Mutating one field on a HashMap key permanently leaks memory.
beats.subline: The map size reports 1, but calling get returns null every single time.
beats.narration: Mutating a field inside a HashMap key after insertion breaks everything. The map keeps the entry in its old bucket, while every subsequent lookup hashes to a brand-new bucket.

beats.title: Java 8 Bucket Treeification Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Converting linked list collision chains into Red-Black trees

nodes.label: Linked List Bucket
nodes.detail: Contains 1 to 7 entries with O(n) scan time

nodes.label: Capacity Check
nodes.detail: If capacity < 64, resizes table instead of building tree

nodes.label: Red-Black Tree
nodes.detail: Converts bucket to tree for guaranteed O(log n) lookups

beats.narration: When a single bucket accumulates 8 colliding nodes, HashMap checks table length. If capacity is under 64, it resizes the table. If 64 or greater, it converts the linked list into a Red-Black tree.

beats.title: The Catastrophic Mutable Key Trap

steps.explanation: Modifying accountId changes future hashCode() output, causing lookup to route to a different bucket.
map.get returns null because it checks the wrong bucket, while size remains 1.

beats.narration: Look at line six. Mutating accountId changes the hash code. When you call map dot get, HashMap inspects the new bucket index, misses completely, and leaves the old entry orphaned in memory.

beats.title: Mutable Keys vs. Immutable Key Record

top.label: Mutable Key Class

bottom.label: Java Record Key

beats.narration: Never use mutable objects as map keys. Standard classes with setters mutate hash values after insertion. Modern Java records enforce final fields, guaranteeing consistent hashing throughout the lifecycle.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Buckets treeify to Red-Black trees at 8 nodes and 64 capacity
Overriding equals without hashCode routes equal keys to wrong buckets
Mutating key fields creates un-removable orphaned memory

beats.headline: LinkedHashMap can build an LRU cache in 10 lines of code.
beats.subline: Overriding a single protected method handles automatic eviction.
beats.narration: Need a Least Recently Used cache without importing heavy third-party libraries? LinkedHashMap has built-in support for access-ordering and automatic entry eviction right out of the box.

beats.title: LinkedHashMap Dual-Structure Architecture
beats.subtitle: Combining O(1) hash lookups with a doubly-linked order chain

nodes.label: Hash Table Array
nodes.detail: Provides O(1) bucket lookups by key like standard HashMap

nodes.label: Doubly-Linked List
nodes.detail: Maintains sequential pointer chain across all map entries

nodes.label: Access Re-Ordering
nodes.detail: get() or put() moves accessed node to the tail of the list

nodes.label: Eldest Eviction
nodes.detail: removeEldestEntry() drops head node when capacity limit hits

beats.narration: LinkedHashMap combines a hash table with a doubly-linked list. When configured with access order true, every read or write moves that entry to the tail, leaving the least recently used entry at the head.

beats.title: Building an LRU Cache with LinkedHashMap

steps.explanation: Passing true to super constructor causes get() and put() to re-order nodes to the tail.
Returning true from removeEldestEntry automatically drops the head node when capacity is exceeded.

beats.narration: By passing true for accessOrder in the super constructor, reading an entry moves it to the tail. Overriding removeEldestEntry returns true when size exceeds maxEntries, evicting the eldest head entry automatically.

beats.title: LinkedHashMap vs. Navigable TreeMap

top.label: LinkedHashMap
top.code:
Map<String, String> cache = 
    new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true);

bottom.label: TreeMap
bottom.code:
NavigableMap<Integer, String> bands = new TreeMap<>();
Integer low = bands.floorKey(450); // returns 100
points: Floor, ceiling, and subMap range queries

beats.narration: LinkedHashMap offers fast O(1) lookups with order tracking. TreeMap uses a Red-Black tree for O(log n) performance, giving you range queries, floor keys, and ceiling keys.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: accessOrder = true turns LinkedHashMap into an access-ordered chain
removeEldestEntry enables simple automatic LRU eviction
TreeMap NavigableMap interface powers floor, ceiling & subMap queries

beats.headline: Why does ConcurrentHashMap ban null keys and values?
beats.subline: HashMap allows nulls, but in multithreaded code null creates dangerous ambiguity.
beats.narration: If ConcurrentHashMap dot get returns null, is the key missing or was it explicitly mapped to null? In a multithreaded environment, calling containsKey next causes a critical race condition.

beats.title: ConcurrentHashMap Concurrency Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Lock-free reads paired with fine-grained bucket synchronization

nodes.label: Volatile Reads
nodes.detail: get() reads volatile node pointers without taking any lock

nodes.label: CAS Insertion
nodes.detail: Atomic Compare-And-Swap places entries into empty buckets

nodes.label: Bucket Lock
nodes.detail: Locks only head node during collisions or updates

nodes.label: Cooperative Resize
nodes.detail: Active threads help migrate buckets during table expansion

beats.narration: ConcurrentHashMap reads volatile node pointers without taking locks. Inserting into an empty bucket uses atomic Compare-And-Swap. Collisions lock only the single bucket head node, allowing other threads to proceed concurrently.

beats.title: Atomic Compound Operations

steps.explanation: Updates values atomically per bucket, eliminating check-then-act race conditions.
Executes mapping function under bucket lock only if key is absent.

beats.narration: Standard check-then-act code creates concurrency bugs. Methods like merge and computeIfAbsent perform atomic updates directly inside the bucket lock, preventing thread contention without extra synchronized blocks.

beats.title: Benchmarking Thread-Safety Strategies
beats.caption: Coarse synchronization vs per-bucket CAS lock-free reads

lines.text: # Comparing Map thread-safety strategies under high concurrency
Note: ConcurrentHashMap forbids null keys & null values by design

beats.narration: Synchronizing an entire map blocks all competing threads. ConcurrentHashMap delivers over thirty times higher throughput by utilizing lock-free volatile reads and per-bucket Compare-And-Swap atomic operations.

beats.title: Chapter Complete! Master Maps
takeaways: ConcurrentHashMap pairs lock-free reads with per-bucket CAS locks
Atomic merge & computeIfAbsent prevent check-then-act race conditions
Null keys & values are banned to eliminate lookup return ambiguity
